abstract: Diffusion virtual try-on (VTO) models produce convincing garment transfers from a single product photograph, but at hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per image every deployment today is offline or falls back to AR mirrors that need a rigged 3D asset per product. We present LiveMirror, a live-camera try-on mirror that renders a flat garment photograph onto a moving person with a diffusion model on one 16 GB consumer GPU. Its core is asynchronous keyframe try-on: generation never blocks the display, every displayed frame is an optical-flow warp of the latest generated keyframe, and keyframes are replaced only through a cross-fade. The display runs at camera rate (25 FPS at 720p) while a new try-on arrives every 370-490 ms; we measure the residual flicker, give a stage-by-stage latency budget, and report which accelerations (step count, consistency LoRA, tiny decoder, compilation) keep garment prints intact. We then show that the same GPU fixes the model's biggest cultural blind spot: try-on models trained on VITON-HD and DressCode render a knee-length kurta or sherwani as a torso-length top or a dress over bare legs. A thigh-covering mask, self-supervised pairs built automatically from 24.9k on-model e-commerce photographs, and 3.2 GPU-hours of attention-only fine-tuning of CatVTON halve the perceptual error on ethnic wear (LPIPS 0.137 to 0.077 on IndoFashion, 0.135 to 0.073 on Atlas; 200 held-out pairs per source) with no regression on Western tops. A two-pass hem-aware mask then removes the remaining failure, recoloured trousers below the hem, on all but 3-4% of pairs at no training cost; in the mirror the hem comes from the previous keyframe for free. The adapted model beats FASHN VTON 1.5 on every aggregate ethnic-wear metric at about $20\times$ lower inference cost, and its weights drop straight into the mirror.
title: LiveMirror: Real-Time Diffusion Virtual Try-On on a Consumer GPU and Its Self-Supervised Adaptation to Indian Ethnic Wear

abstract: Overparameterized neural networks can represent the same function through many different hidden configurations, raising the question of which representation is favored by a given training algorithm. We study how stochastic gradient descent (SGD), jointly training both layers, resolves this ambiguity in finite-width, bias-free, two-layer ReLU networks trained to learn a linear teacher under Gaussian inputs. At width two, exact fitting leaves no choice: the neurons must align with the teacher directions. At every width $m \ge 4$, however, infinitely many non-aligned exact fits are possible. Despite this ambiguity, we prove that joint batch-size-one SGD from sufficiently small initialization drives every neuron arbitrarily close to one of the two teacher directions while reaching arbitrarily small population error in finite time. This occurs without explicit regularization, layerwise training, gradient clipping, or a learning-rate schedule. The dynamics additionally select an initialization-dependent allocation of the fitted function across neurons, providing a finer characterization of the representation selected by SGD. Numerical experiments reproduce the predicted alignment, fitting, and initialization-dependent allocation. Our results identify sufficient conditions under which standard SGD exhibits a strong implicit bias toward a highly structured internal representation, even when overparameterization creates infinitely many qualitatively different exact representations.
title: SGD Selects Initialization-Dependent Representation in Overparameterized ReLU Networks

abstract: We study when the coefficients of a linearly parameterized analytic system can be identified from a single input-solution pair. Given a finite dictionary of analytic operators, each admissible input induces a finite-dimensional linear recovery map from coefficients to observed outputs. Coefficient recovery is possible exactly when this map is injective. We define the degenerate input set as the set of inputs for which injectivity fails and prove a zero-one law: either every admissible input is degenerate, or the degenerate set is negligible in the sense that it is compactly slice-null and has zero measure under every nondegenerate Gaussian measure. We then apply this framework to the recovery of matrices, analytic continuous-time dynamical systems, and differential operators. For several ODE and PDE classes, we further characterize the degenerate sets explicitly and identify deterministic choices of inputs that guarantee recovery.
title: One-shot identification of analytic systems

abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning while inexpensive generative sampling supports policy optimization, providing an effective approach to experience-based post-training of flow-based VLAs.
title: OVOGO: Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Recent work on Large Language Models (LLMs) suggests that reasoning capabilities can be enhanced at test time not only through longer token-level reasoning traces, but also through additional computation in latent space. This raises a natural question for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): can additional computation in latent space improve visual perception at test time? In this work, we first verify that MLLMs contain stable reusable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting normal generation. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{Lo}ok \textbf{Ba}ck in the \textbf{L}atent \textbf{S}pace (\textbf{Lobals}), a training-free decoding method that identifies the contiguous layer window with the strongest visual-token attention and re-forwards through it, allowing the model to revisit visual evidence in latent space. We demonstrate that this latent-space revisit strategy can improve MLLMs' performance across diverse multimodal settings, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks.
title: Test-Time Latent Computation to Improve Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) does not change the optimal policy, but how much it speeds up learning depends on the potential and on effects outside this guarantee. We analyse how PBRS changes the one-step reward while it preserves the discounted return: a per-step $(γ-1)Φ$ term, the terminal-state rule, a constant shift of the potential, and positive cycles in a bonus that is not potential-based. We then measure these consequences in pre-registered experiments with a PPO agent. The agent has a limited egocentric view and is tested on two MiniGrid navigation tasks (160 runs, 10 seeds per condition). On LavaCrossing, a geodesic (BFS) potential learned faster than both the sparse baseline and a Euclidean potential with a 7x7 and a 5x5 view (AUC difference +0.27 to +0.39, Holm p between 0.007 and 0.0499). The Euclidean potential did not differ from the baseline. In 20 runs with a non-potential bonus, none of the agents learned the task. The Euclidean potential caused more than twice as many deaths in lava during early training. View size did not detectably change the benefit of shaping. With a 5x5 view on SimpleCrossing, some BFS runs got stuck in loops and never learned; shifting the potential did not remove this, so the per-step term alone does not explain it.
title: Policy Invariance Is Not Learning Invariance: Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Navigation with a Limited View

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.
title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers

abstract: An assistant that summarizes old conversations may later need a detail from the original exchange. It can score archived passages against the question, but only passages that fit in the prompt reach the answering model. We tested whether a BM25 filter saves input tokens once that limit is taken into account. We calibrated the filter on passages that individually corrected an answer the model got wrong from the summaries alone. Across 75 LongMemEval questions, filtering changed one prompt and saved 0.096% of input tokens. With and without the filter, the model answered the same questions correctly under a second automated grading. On a random sample, two human graders' settled judgments agreed with the automated grades in 92.9% of definite comparisons (Cohen's kappa = 0.805). Building on earlier work that distinguishes retrieved evidence from delivered evidence, we give an exact test for packers that try whole passages in a fixed order and skip any that do not fit. Run the packer without the filter. The prompt changes exactly when an admitted passage scores below the cutoff. Code and data: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Certfold
title: Why Calibrated BM25 Filtering Barely Reduced Context on LongMemEval

abstract: MMORPGs continually face automated programs (bots) that disrupt gameplay balance and in-game economies. An unsupervised Transformer framework can mine collectively behaving bot groups, but its multi-GPU training is costly in live operations. We show that such GPU-trained sequence models are not strictly necessary for this task. Our CPU pipeline pairs zone embeddings learned from movement context, which place teleport-linked zones close together, with a training-free coordinate kernel, and then applies density clustering. It trains 3-5$\times$ faster than the GPU-based Transformer (56-86$\times$ on the same CPU) while matching its mining quality on two commercial MMORPGs, and has been deployed since late 2024. We also share deployment lessons on how to set the clustering threshold and when to retrain.
title: A CPU-Only Framework for Mining Collectively-Behaving Bots in MMORPGs

abstract: Continual pre-training (\textit{CPT}) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (\textit{MCQA}) accuracy alone, offering only a narrow view of how adaptation unfolds. We jointly track factual knowledge via \textit{MCQA} and open-ended behavior via pairwise preference rankings across $18$ checkpoints for each of eight instruction-tuned \textit{Qwen} models ($0.5B$ to $8B$), adapted to German medicine with \textit{CPT} and \textit{SLERP} merging. The two axes converge at consistently different rates, with preference rankings reaching $90\%$ of their total gain after a median of $1.7B$ tokens versus $3.5B$ for \textit{MCQA}. A judge-free token-distribution measure reaches this threshold at $1.9B$ tokens. Per-aspect scores indicate that these early preference gains largely reflect surface alignment, meaning models can sound domain-appropriate before their factual knowledge catches up. Larger adapted models close more of the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, whereas preference gain per FLOP falls by about an order of magnitude across our size range. We therefore argue that judge-based preference scores, which can plateau while \textit{MCQA} knowledge is still improving, should not be used alone to infer adaptation convergence or domain readiness.
title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? An Empirical Study of Decoupled Knowledge and Generation Trajectories in Clinical LLMs

abstract: Odor perception arises from a combinatorial code in which each molecule activates a specific subset of olfactory receptors (ORs), and the resulting activation pattern determines the perceived smell. We present a framework for de novo generation of molecules predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles. We first construct a panoramic binding matrix over 20 ORs, then cluster it to discover representative activation patterns, and finally formulate a structured selectivity loss, combining pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints, to steer a molecular generator via reinforcement learning. Across nine target profiles of varying complexity, our method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18000 oracle calls and provides the largest gains on profiles that are rare under the prior, especially broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets.
title: De Novo Generation of Odorant Molecules with Targeted Olfactory Receptor Activation Patterns

abstract: This report presents a comprehensive pipeline for developing an end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving model for the Physical AI AV Track. The framework consists of data curation, HD map auto-labelling, data-driven imitation learning, and simulator-based reinforcement learning. To ensure safety in the closed-loop setting, we introduce a selection-based E2E planning approach that leverages object detection and BEV segmentation to filter out trajectory candidates likely to cause collisions or off-road driving. Trained on NVIDIA NuRec and the NVIDIA PAI-AV dataset, our method scores a fixed vocabulary of trajectory candidates for collision, drivable-area compliance, and progress learned from simulated rollouts, and selects the best candidate that passes the filter. This design highlights the effectiveness of combining E2E planning with perception-based trajectory filtering for safe and reliable closed-loop autonomous driving.
title: AXE: AlpaSim E2E Closed Loop Challenge Technical Report

abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.
title: JEPA-ICL: Progress-Aligned Latent Plans for In-Context Robotic Manipulation

abstract: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering judgment: flagging hidden hazards and avoiding needless work.
title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?

abstract: Automated verification of industrial assembly processes remains a challenging problem due to substantial visual variability, limited availability of labeled defect data, and the fine-grained nature of many assembly errors. Existing approaches often rely on object detection, CAD models, or supervised classification pipelines, which can struggle to generalize across changing products and assembly configurations. In this work, we propose a novel self-supervised assembly verification framework based on Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs). Starting from the JEPA-based world model LeWorldModel, we investigate how the architecture must be adapted to verify the correctness of fine-grained assembly operations. To this end, we formulate assembly verification as a predictive world modeling task operating on before-and-after observations of assembly processes. Experimental results on industrial assembly tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach reliably detects both fine-grained incorrect assembly states and action-state mismatches, achieving an AUROC of 86.9% on a newly introduced assembly verification dataset. These results indicate that JEPA-based predictive representations constitute a promising foundation for robust and data-efficient industrial assembly verification.
title: Assembly-JEPA: Using World Models for Fine-Grained Industrial Image Verification

abstract: Diffusion models memorize training images and reproduce them almost verbatim when prompted, creating copyright and privacy liabilities. Data unlearning erases the influence of specific training samples from a trained model without retraining, and is two-sided: it must forget the targets while preserving generation quality on everything else. Prior methods use the squared-L2 diffusion loss, at most with a hand-set frequency mask; however, it is known that every Bregman divergence is a mathematically valid choice and the squared-L2 is only the simplest example. BEND is the first to search this family: it fits a spectral Bregman divergence to the unlearning task through a bilevel loop, so the loss itself is shaped to forget thoroughly while protecting quality. It also redirects a memorized image to the mean of its retain images, where ReTrack, the state of the art, redirects it to a single near-copy. On Stable Diffusion, a single BEND model erases all 48 verifiably memorized benchmark images at once. It forgets at least as much as per-target, sequential, and jointly trained ReTrack (SSCD 0.084 versus 0.094-0.120), at the quality of the model before unlearning (CLIP-IQA 0.81 versus 0.64-0.69). BEND also outperforms the state of the art on CelebA-HQ in all three measures of the benchmark, and matches or exceeds it on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
title: BEND: Spectral Bregman Losses for Multi-Image Unlearning in Diffusion Models

abstract: While frontier language models are becoming capable cybersecurity assistants, they also create a dual-use cyber risk: the same capabilities that help defenders identify and analyze vulnerabilities can similarly help attackers weaponize them. Existing cyber benchmarks measure either raw offensive capability or generic refusal behavior, overlooking the dual-use cyber assessment of preserving benign security utility while refusing assistance that materially advances misuse. We introduce CyberDualEval, a benchmark with 430 vulnerable tasks for measuring dual-use cyber risk in frontier language models. Each task is decomposed into three phases of increasing operationalization: security analysis, proof-of-concept generation, and exploit generation. To quantify the residual cyber risk, we annotate each task with a Task Weaponization Score that measures how much work remains to turn the resulting artifact into unauthorized cyber misuse. CyberDualEval assesses ten closed- and open-weight language models both on correct compliance and on task performance, developing four deterministic mechanisms for determining per-phase success on a large subset of the dataset. Our evaluation reveals that none of the existing frontier models effectively navigate helping with safe requests and refusing risky ones, characterized by being overly-cautious. On the other hand, recent open-weight models rarely refuse and demonstrate strong validated accuracy on risky requests.
title: CyberDualEval: Measuring Dual-Use Cyber Risks in Frontier Language Models

abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
title: DelayOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation from a Synchronous Teacher for Real-time Asynchronous Policies

abstract: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.
title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode

abstract: In text to image AI models, fixing the prompt and the random seed is widely assumed to fix the image. We show that it does not on GPUs. We evaluate six text-to-image models (diffusion and autoregressive) under four numerical precisions and quantizations on three GPU types (RTX A6000, RTX 6000 Ada, and H100 NVL), across up to 100 prompts per set for all six models. For each configuration we compare, with the prompt and seed fixed, the image generated alone with the image generated inside a batch, and we also compare across GPUs. Every replay control reported here is bit-exact, so the variation is not random noise: the execution setting, mainly the batch composition and the GPU, decides the output. The effect is large and model dependent. Structural similarity between the single-image and the batched output falls to 0.580 for an autoregressive model in bf16 and to 0.551 with int8. For a second autoregressive model in bf16 it falls to 0.261 with sampled decoding and to 0.229 with greedy decoding, and for an fp8 diffusion model to 0.68. A diffusion model in bf16 stays close to the batch-1 output (0.96-0.98) but changes every image. In most cases the batched image is a different but equally valid image; in some, such as prompts with digits and counters, it is visibly worse. Cross-GPU differences are of the same order as the batch effect: for one autoregressive model in bf16 compared across two GPU architectures (RTX 6000 Ada versus RTX A6000), no image is bit-identical and the cross-GPU LPIPS (0.355 to 0.383) matches the batch effect within one GPU (0.347 to 0.381). The consequences are direct: seeds do not make results reproducible, benchmarks and image-quality comparisons that mix batch sizes or hardware can be biased, and safety audits and A/B tests on generated images need the serving setup reported.
title: Reproducible by Seed? Not on GPUs: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models

abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and preserves \textbf{\color{blue}90.4\%} of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.
title: Body and Soul: Decoupling Robotic Brain and Policy with RoboHarness-Zero

abstract: Neural networks (NNs) have been increasingly used as function approximators, motivating the study of the geometry of their function spaces. We study the set of functions represented by shallow neural networks with hyperbolic tangent activation, fixed input and output dimensions, and $n$ hidden neurons. In particular, we prove that the subset represented by irreducible networks in the sense of Sussmann (Neural Networks, 1992), i.e., networks with no redundant neurons, is a smooth embedded submanifold of the Sobolev spaces $\mathrm{W}^{\ell,p}$ on bounded sets for any $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\in[1,+\infty]$. The key step is to show that if a sequence of networks converges in $\mathrm{W}^{\ell,p}$ to an irreducible network with the same number of hidden neurons, then the parameters of the approximating networks remain bounded. Finally, we show that this manifold has exactly $n+1$ connected components when both the input and output are scalar, and is connected otherwise.
title: Irreducible shallow tanh neural networks are a manifold

abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.
title: Near-Far Attention: Region-Aware Sparse Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Decoding

abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($π_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation

abstract: Splitting notions for conditional belief bases aim at localizing reasoning and computation tasks to subbases containing only the relevant parts of the belief base. Among the different reasoning mechanisms, c-representations, a special kind of Spohn's ranking models, have been shown to provide high-quality inferences. c-Representations can be conveniently specified via a constraint satisfaction problem. In this article, we introduce the notion of conditional constraint splittings, extending constraint splittings by also allowing the subbases to share conditionals. Taking inspiration from conditional syntax splittings, we identify the subclasses of safe and fully localized conditional constraint splittings, allowing us to locally and independently solve the constraint system on the subbases. We also generalize solution splittings for c-representations to safe conditional c-solution splittings and provide an in-depth analysis of their relationship to conditional constraint splittings. Additionally, we elaborate on the relationship of these new splitting notions to safe and generalized safe conditional syntax splittings and also to safe covers, which have been proposed for localized computation of c-representations.
title: Splitting Belief Bases Conditionally based on Constraints for c-Representations and their Solutions

abstract: We introduce JONES-19, a high-quality image dataset documenting 1,901 ornament designs belonging to nineteen human cultures. The images and their annotations are based on an open access archive of The Grammar of Ornament (London, 1856), by Owen Jones. The dataset poses numerous challenges as a benchmark for computer vision classification tasks and for research at the intersection of machine learning and art and design: a small sample size, image samples of human-designed artifacts rather than common objects in-context or natural scenes, imbalanced class distribution, and image distinctions based on fine details involving line patterns, reliefs, and colors. As a design-inspired dataset, JONES-19 can serve as a benchmark for various research fields, such as visual recognition, data-efficient learning, art-historical research, architectural style analysis, and cultural heritage. This paper describes the curation of the JONES-19 dataset and reports a baseline classification benchmark that evaluates the suitability of the dataset for training classifiers and exposes insights into inter-class relationships--particularly cultural similarities--by examining patterns in misclassification errors. The dataset and its accompanying documentation are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/harvardseas-cultural-ornaments/JONES-19.
title: JONES-19: A Cultural Image Dataset Based on The Grammar of Ornament

abstract: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to 13.7% and required state-check failures from 63 to 1 across 180 trials. The resulting policy outperforms seven reference baselines by over 20 points while reducing output tokens by 17-39% across seven of eight external benchmarks without regressing on general reasoning or tool use.
title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents

abstract: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.
title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models

abstract: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.
title: VeriTouch: Verified Visuo-Tactile World Models that Improve Robot Policy Learning

abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.
title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data

abstract: We consider the problem of learning microscopic traffic dynamics and reconstructing vehicle trajectories from section entry/exit timestamps (EET) recorded by cameras and from the positions of a probe vehicle leading the platoon. The dynamics are difficult to recover as each vehicle's position is measured only at two points, and its trajectory between them is unknown. By combining Neural ODEs with a local density approximation, we learn a follow-the-leader model whose speed--density relation is a neural network. With such sparse data, an unconstrained network may learn physically unrealistic relations, such as negative speeds or non-zero speeds on a fully congested road. We therefore introduce a normalization that, applied to a monotone neural network with a learned regime change, enforces the endpoint conditions, guaranteeing an admissible speed--density relation while provably retaining the ability to approximate any admissible one. We validate the method on first- and second-order simulations, recovering the speed--density relation of the first-order model and reconstructing the trajectories of both models, with mean maximum position errors of 2.50~m and 2.51~m, respectively, on a 125~m road segment. On real-world ring-road data, the proposed model still yields an admissible relation, whereas both baselines violate the constraints; the large spread in the data, however, highlights the limitations of a first-order model with homogeneous driver behaviors.
title: Physics-Constrained Neural ODEs for Learning Traffic Dynamics and Trajectories from Road Entry/Exit Times

abstract: As the intelligence of an AI agent increases relative to a trusted monitor, so does the risk that the monitor will fail to understand the agent's actions or to evaluate them confidently. We introduce interrogation protocols to a high-stakes AI control setting, and allow the monitor to ask the untrusted agent questions about confusing actions. For interrogation to improve safety, a weaker model must be able to distinguish misleading explanations produced by an attack policy from genuine ones produced by an honest policy. We find that on a held-out subset of BashArena, an interrogation protocol improves safety at a 1% audit budget from 72.6% for an actions-only baseline, which does not use interrogations, to 79.5% (+7.0 pp [+0.9, +20.1], 95% paired bootstrap interval), but most of this uplift can be captured by having a trusted model state a specific concern. More broadly, our work suggests that interrogating agents can improve safety, allowing monitors to catch more attacks at a larger capability gap.
title: Interrogation Protocols for AI Control

abstract: Although technical analysis remains widely used in practice, the need for manually constructed indicators is increasingly questioned as deep learning models can extract features directly from OHLC price data. This paper examines the standalone economic value of trading volume and manually constructed technical-indicator groups and whether adding these groups to OHLC candlestick charts provides incremental economic value. Using daily data for 1,707 Chinese A-share stocks from 2013 to 2025, we construct approximately 3.36 million stock-window samples and encode them as multi-channel images containing candlestick charts, trading volume, and seven widely used manually constructed technical indicators. The primary analysis uses a 2D CNN on these images; complementary tests apply a logistic regression, a 1D CNN, and an LSTM to numerical representations of the same samples. Out-of-sample performance from 2021 to 2025 is evaluated using decile portfolios, Sharpe ratios, Fama--French alphas, and formal pairwise tests. Our empirical results yield two central findings. First, specifications based separately on OHLC, trading volume, and each technical-indicator group produce significantly positive high-minus-low returns and factor-adjusted alphas, together with economically meaningful Sharpe ratios; the OHLC-only specifications generally perform best under the nonlinear models. Second, adding these technical-indicator groups to OHLC does not systematically improve any of these performance measures in our setting. Together, these results provide the first large-scale evidence from the Chinese A-share market on the standalone and incremental economic value of these technical-indicator groups across multiple representations and model architectures.
title: Do Candlestick Charts Suffice? The Incremental Economic Value of Technical Indicators in Stock Return Prediction

abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training quantization of dLLMs has so far been calibrated and evaluated under fixed-step samplers without caching. We study W4A4 quantization under the deployed decoder and find that the decoder determines both where quantization harms accuracy and what it costs. Irreversible errors enter chiefly through forced commitments, made when no position clears the threshold: they are a minority of commitments but carry most quantization-induced flips. Quantization also levies a parallelism tax, extra forward passes per response: by compressing top logit gaps, it pushes positions below the threshold while leaving predictions largely intact. We propose DECAL, which reweights layer-wise calibration by a commitment-risk prior measured on the deployed decoder, and an argmax-preserving commit temperature that recovers the tax. On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL attains the best average accuracy among W4A4 methods, with lower run-to-run variance than the closest existing calibration method.
title: Quantizing Diffusion LLMs under Parallel Decoding: Commitment Risk and the Parallelism Tax

abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.
title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate harmful or sensitive content, such as pornographic or violent imagery, raising serious security concerns. Model editing has recently emerged as an efficient approach to mitigate this issue. It modifies pretrained models with minimal parameter updates to alter specific concepts while preserving overall model capabilities. However, due to the entangled representations of different concepts in diffusion models, direct modifications inevitably disrupt non-target concepts. Meanwhile, U-Net's hierarchical heterogeneity hinders unified strategies from balancing erasure and quality. To address these issues, we propose Hierarchical Orthogonal Subspace Erasure (HOSE). This method projects parameter updates into the subspace orthogonal to general knowledge, thereby eliminating interference with non-target concepts. Considering the hierarchical heterogeneity of the U-Net architecture, we further propose a hierarchical adaptive mechanism, constructing differentiated subspace projections for different layers to precisely adapt to the model's hierarchical structure, thereby resolving the inherent trade-off between erasure and image quality in unified constraints. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method reduces harmful content generation by 80% compared with the unedited model. While it inevitably incurs some image quality degradation, it still outperforms other editing-based baselines in terms of quality preservation, and achieves a significantly better trade-off between harmful content suppression and quality loss than these baselines. Notably, our approach demonstrates higher adversarial robustness than existing SOTA method, indicating that the target concepts have been more thoroughly erased. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sevenqiiu/HOSE.
title: HOSE: Hierarchical Orthogonal Subspace Erasure for Concept Unlearning in Diffusion Models

abstract: Diabetes leads to several health complications throughout the body, with the complication in the eyes being Diabetic Retinopathy. It leads to damaging or abnormal changes in the blood vessels' structure, causing vision loss. The need for massive screening of a large population of diabetic patients has created a necessity for computer-aided, fully automatic diagnosis of DR. CNNs have shown great promise in the classification of DR based on the Fundus images. Building a reliable model faces considerable challenges due to the limited availability of high-quality annotated datasets and issues with varying image quality and class imbalances. This paper aims to demonstrate the UNET, and its Stacked Architecture variant and their performance across several datasets. This paper has compared and studied the UNET architecture's performance across multiple stacks and has come to a soft conclusion that the architecture performs its best at three stacks, and any more leads to deterioration of its performance. The model aims at classifying the images into five categories, 0 to 4, where 0 is no DR, and 4 is proliferative DR.
title: Advancements in Diabetic Retinopathy Classification Using Novel Multi-Stacked U-Net Architectures

abstract: Coordinating vessels through the shared waterways of busy ports grows more challenging as vessel traffic increases. Port authorities need realistic simulations to assess how arrival schedules, anchorage assignments, and routes affect vessel throughput and navigation safety. Existing AIS-based trajectory models predict a vessel's track from its past trajectory in an open-loop fashion. They do not simulate step-by-step responses to other ships or test whether a vessel collides or reaches its goal. To address this problem, we introduce JaxNaviSim, a data-driven simulator and learning benchmark coupling Automatic Identification System (AIS) data with fast, controllable traffic simulation, in which learned models steer vessels through recorded traffic. First, we release a dataset of ~141 million AIS records from over 30K vessels across eight high-density regions of the Singapore Strait, among the world's busiest waterways, with ~6.7 million vessel-hours. Unlike several existing AIS datasets which mostly cover open seas, ours captures close-quarters vessel traffic in the narrow strait. Second, we define a navigation task for each recorded vessel trajectory. A model steers that vessel every 10 s from its recorded state to its anchoring point or region exit, while surrounding ships follow their recorded tracks or are steered by the model. We implement a JAX simulator that runs these tasks in large batches on a GPU. We also incorporate multiple vessel dynamics models and sea surface currents. Finally, we benchmark imitation learning (IL), offline and online RL, and include Predictive Action Refinement (PAR) as a safety baseline that cuts collision rates to 1-3%. The comparison shows that low tracking error does not ensure arrival, and learned policies can reach most destinations yet collide in 20-45% of episodes.
title: JaxNaviSim: A GPU-Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator and Learning Benchmark for Maritime Navigation

abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.
title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data

abstract: Diffusion-based graph generation models progressively transform Gaussian noise into structured graphs through stochastic dynamics. We observe that the effectiveness of this transformation is fundamentally determined by the evolution of the diffusion trajectory. Existing graph diffusion models often suffer from excessive uncertainty during diffusion and delayed growth of the signal-to-noise ratio, causing useful structural information to emerge only in the later stages of generation. To address this issue, we propose the Vasicek Graph Diffusion (VGD), a graph diffusion process derived from the Vasicek dynamics. The key insight of VGD is data-anchored mean dynamics with a closed-form solution, which analytically establishes a continuous transition from Gaussian noise to the target graph distribution. Unlike conventional graph diffusion processes that rely predominantly on stochastic evolution, VGD introduces a data-anchored drift that continuously steers the latent state toward the target distribution throughout diffusion. As a consequence, VGD maintains a smoothly evolving uncertainty while rapidly increasing the signal-to-noise ratio throughout diffusion, allowing informative graph structures to emerge much earlier during generation. Extensive experiments on multiple graph generation benchmarks demonstrate that VGD outperforms existing diffusion-based graph generative models in terms of generation quality and structural fidelity.
title: Vasicek Graph Diffusion Model

abstract: Invariant causal prediction identifies the direct causes of a target $Y$ by searching for covariate sets whose conditional law of $Y$ is stable across environments. We state that criterion at the level of operators, calling a set $S$ invariant when the conditional mean embeddings of $Y$ given $X_S$ agree across environments, and characterise the resulting family exactly: under two conditions on the environments, which we state separately because they fail independently, the invariant sets are precisely those containing $PA(Y)$ and no descendant of $Y$. Two consequences follow. Invariance does not identify $PA(Y)$ uniquely, since every descendant-free superset is invariant as well; and $PA(Y)$ is the unique minimal invariant set. In finite samples, recovery requires the non-invariant sets to be separated from invariance by a margin, and the sample size splits into a screening term logarithmic in the ambient dimension and a term inherited from conditional mean embedding estimation, which is the binding one. The characterisation yields two selection rules with different failure modes, of which the conservative one controls false positives. Controlled experiments verify each population prediction directly, including the failure of uniqueness. They also show that invariance testing is a practical bottleneck: two natural designs are severely miscalibrated, while the selected test reduces but does not eliminate Type I error inflation.
title: What Environment Invariance Identifies: Minimal Invariant Sets in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

abstract: Geometry Problem Solving (GPS) serves as a rigorous test of the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly when solutions require auxiliary constructions absent from the input diagram. However, explicit diagramming methods suffer from unstable image generation quality and cascading errors, while existing implicit attention mechanisms primarily focus on visible elements, limiting their ability to support reasoning that requires additional geometric constructions. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{AuxCA} (Auxiliary-Clues-Aware GRPO), a reinforcement learning framework that helps models learn transferable auxiliary-construction strategies that can be applied beyond the training domain without explicit diagram generation at inference time. Specifically, we introduce Auxiliary Clues Dependency (\textbf{ACD}) to quantify the influence of auxiliary visual clues on token generation and integrate it into GRPO through fine-grained advantage weighting. Furthermore, we incorporate an auxiliary incentive reward to encourage the effective use of auxiliary geometric clues in correct solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AuxCA-8B outperforms the explicit-plotting baseline Bagel-Canvas and achieves competitive performance with leading proprietary models on auxiliary-dependent plane geometry problems. Improvements on analytic geometry, solid geometry, and external benchmarks further suggest that the learned strategies can transfer beyond the training domain. Code is available at https://github.com/fukua23/AuxCA
title: Auxiliary Clues Aware's Geometry Problem Solving

abstract: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.
title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models

abstract: LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. When the guard and the executor choose differently, the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one. We introduce this attack, tool-call smuggling, and study it across the stack. We describe six ways in which the same bytes yield different calls and build a differential testing harness that gives identical bytes to 17 pinned parser and validator configurations; most pairs disagree on some inputs, and even two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs. On tasks from $τ$-bench and AgentDojo, an attacker who can rewrite the bytes in transit cancels another customer's reservation and creates a file that the guard blocks by name, while the audit log names only the approved call. Content the model reads splits guard and executor only inside a string: ten models we test write no repeated or disguised key into the call itself where we see it, but copy one verbatim into JSON text in an argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legitimate tool's public schema and adding one field, which a note explains, gets the model to fill it, unseen by the guard, with user data. Parsing each call once, JSON text included, keeping only the fields of the approved schema, and handing it to the executor, sealed with its call ID in transit, stops all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack we built.
title: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents

abstract: An $\varepsilon$-omnipredictor uses one forecast for an entire family of downstream losses. After postprocessing for each loss, its expected loss must be at most $\varepsilon$ above that of the best comparator for that loss. A binary single-index model (SIM) learns a norm-bounded weight vector $w$ and a nondecreasing link $ρ$. It reduces the features $x$ to one linear score $w^\top x$, then maps that score to a probability $p(x)=ρ(w^\top x)$. Hu, Tian, and Yang (STOC 2025) achieved $\varepsilon$-omniprediction for binary matching losses using $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ SIMs and asked whether one SIM suffices. In the population model, we prove that one SIM suffices for exact omniprediction in their bounded-action setting. The result holds for any compact family of continuous nondecreasing target links. With unrestricted actions and matching losses generated by $1/β$-strongly convex entropies, the SIM's link can also be $β$-Lipschitz. For $K$ classes and $d$-dimensional features with finite first moment, $\min\{d,K-1\}$ linear scores are necessary and sufficient in the worst case. A joint link maps these scores to class probabilities, and its Lipschitz bound $β$ is also sharp under the comparator's coefficient norm bound. For bounded features and smooth entropies, we achieve $\varepsilon$-omniprediction for two or three classes using $\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ samples at fixed confidence and regularity. This bound is independent of $d$ and tight up to logarithmic factors. For any fixed number of classes $K \ge 2$, the tight worst-case sample complexity for $\varepsilon$-omniprediction under the Dirichlet condition on the features is $Θ_K(1/\varepsilon^2)$.
title: Omniprediction with the Minimum Number of Linear Scores

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.
title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at individual robotic skills, yet integrating heterogeneous skills into a single policy remains a key challenge for general-purpose robotic control, especially in whole-body tasks with differing manipulation and locomotion requirements. Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations.
title: GeoMerge-OPD: Balanced Skill Integration in Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention

abstract: Finite mixture regression is sensitive to gross residual outliers when component errors are modeled by Gaussian likelihoods. We propose a log-truncated likelihood for mixture regression. The likelihood is obtained by integrating a logarithmically growing Catoni-type score and exponentiating the negative integrated score, producing a proper location-scale density with a reusable normalizing constant and EM-compatible responsibilities. Although the induced density itself is lighter than exponential and has all moments, its likelihood score grows only logarithmically; this distinction yields a smooth residual-robust estimator that can be stably fitted when the data are generated from Laplace, Pareto, or even infinite-variance heavy-tailed error mechanisms. We derive deterministic tail envelopes, the location-scale decomposition of the normalizing constant, a rejection sampler, a lower-bounded mixing-weight update, a unique componentwise scale update, and a constrained generalized EM algorithm. The theory gives monotonicity of the observed likelihood and a local population-to-sample perturbation guarantee under standard compactness, contraction, and numerical-accuracy conditions. Simulations and applications to insurance claim severity and crypto return innovations show that the method is a competitive smooth likelihood-based alternative to Gaussian and pseudo-robust EM procedures, especially in residual-outlier regimes, while also clarifying its limitations under high leverage and extremely adversarial contamination.
title: Robust Mixture Regressions and EM Algorithms via the Log-Truncated Likelihood

abstract: Behavior-cloning policies show strong ability in sequential control by generating coherent multi-step action chunks, yet their purely imitative objective limits zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks. While offline reinforcement learning offers principled policy improvement, existing methods either require task-specific reward supervision or remain tied to a specific actor during critic training or policy deployment, inflating training cost and restricting cross-policy generalization. We observe that evaluating actions under the data-collecting behavior largely preserves their relative value ordering across target policies, offering a way around actor coupling. Combining this property with reward-free successor prediction, we propose Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations (ABI) to learn multi-horizon action-chunk representations from unlabeled trajectories without reward supervision or actor training. At test time, pairing the frozen representation with lightweight task readouts forms a chunk critic that guides target policies without parameter updates and transfers directly across distinct unseen policies. Our analysis establishes when the value ordering is preserved across policies and when selecting among proposed chunks improves closed-loop return. Across 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, ABI's chunk critic guides weak imitation policies to match or surpass zero-shot RL baselines with high sample efficiency, outperforms existing zero-shot critics on identical proposals, and improves externally trained RL actors without retraining. From raw pixels, ABI delivers substantial guidance gains and surpasses prior zero-shot RL baselines on visual manipulation, highlighting its potential for visuomotor control.
title: ABI: Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations for Zero-Shot Test-Time Guidance

abstract: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench
title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?

abstract: Existing methods for assessing training data contamination in Large Language Models achieve high accuracy, but fundamentally rely on gray-box access, rendering them inapplicable to fully black-box environments. This limitation forces auditors to rely on full-sequence sampling or rigid heuristics, both of which incur prohibitive inference costs and struggle to isolate the underlying memorization signal. To overcome this, we propose a generation-based black-box framework that infers context-induced information gain from targeted token discrepancies. We introduce a budget-constrained auditing regime, building on the empirical observation that the membership signal is highly sparse and concentrated in a few highly informative tokens. We formalize this sparsity, showing why uniform sampling needs many more samples than a policy that targets informative positions. Empirically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art black-box separation accuracy while needing about 3x fewer queries than uniform position sampling. Finally, we apply this methodology to closed frontier models, exploring its capacity and limits in surfacing potential training data overlaps on commercial APIs.
title: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination

abstract: This paper proposes the model-agnostic Multi-Task Learning Multi-Head Online Learning (MTL-MHOL) framework for conversion rate (CVR) prediction. Existing approaches typically address key challenges in CVR prediction, such as delayed feedback and data sparsity, in isolation or lack flexibility and practical applicability. MTL-MHOL adopts a time bucketing approach to account for delayed feedback and combines it with multi-task learning of an auxiliary task to mitigate data sparsity. We evaluate the framework on proprietary datasets from a private company and on a public dataset from Criteo. MTL-MHOL matches or outperforms all benchmark models in terms of Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) and Relative Cross Entropy (RCE), and it correctly captures temporal trends in the data using an MLP backbone, while maintaining strong performance with a DeepFM backbone. In particular, MTL-MHOL matches the performance of the advanced delayed-feedback method FSIW, outperforms the entire-space approach ESMM by 21.5% in RCE, and achieves up to 81% lift in RCE compared to the best-performing classical benchmark.
title: MTL-MHOL: Predicting Online Conversions under Delayed Feedback and Data Sparsity

abstract: Learning how actions change visual states is essential for prediction and decision-making in embodied tasks. Existing action-conditioned JEPA world models typically predict future representations at discrete observation intervals, leaving the temporal evolution of action effects implicit.
