We introduce ActField, a continuous-time JEPA world model that explicitly models latent state evolution through an action-conditioned vector field integrated over physical time. ActField separates action-independent evolution from action-induced changes, with the latter modulated by the latent context. A reference-conditioned representation and multi-step dynamics loss further support accurate long-horizon prediction. Together, these components provide a structured and temporally continuous formulation for predicting action-conditioned visual dynamics. Experiments across LIBERO, DROID, and BEHAVIOR demonstrate improved visual prediction fidelity and more accurate action-induced motion prediction over existing world models. Further evaluations on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the utility of ActField in improving downstream policy planning through VLM-guided action selection.
title: ActField: Learning Action Effects as Continuous-Time Latent Dynamics

abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.
title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce

abstract: Tuning a mixed-integer programming (MIP) solver is an instance-specific problem, where a poor configuration can increase solving time by orders of magnitude. Existing Bayesian optimization tuners treat solver tuning as a black-box optimization problem: each evaluation returns a single score, allowing the tuner to learn which configuration is faster, but not why. Inspired by the use of profilers in GPU-kernel optimization, we introduce APEC (Agent for Per-instance Explainable Configuration), a log-grounded tuning agent for MIP solvers. APEC has three layers: a deterministic layer that profiles each log, an interpretation layer that guides hypothesis-driven diagnosis, and a system layer that controls evaluation, enabling more reliable and interpretable solver tuning. On the full MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set, APEC achieves a 1.58X improvement over the default configuration with over 38% fewer parameter changes than the baselines, making the results easier to read.
title: Beyond the Black Box: A Diagnosis-Driven Agent for Interpretable MIP Solver Tuning

abstract: Large language models can have behaviours which only arise in hard-to-anticipate contexts. These hidden behaviours pose a challenge to alignment audits, which seek to uncover problematic model behaviour but are limited by the scenarios the auditor can anticipate. To address this challenge, we explore limited-parameter finetuning (LPF) on examples of a target behaviour. While training 3-25% of LoRA parameters, LPF reveals whether the model has a hidden behaviour, even when standard behavioural evaluations cannot. LPF succeeds on a suite of model organisms with hidden behaviours (8-14B parameters), and also surfaces naturally occurring hidden behaviours in open-weight models (27-35B parameters). LPF can thus distinguish between models which appear behaviourally identical to an auditor, and does not require the context in which the hidden behaviour surfaces. LPF provides a novel affordance that may be useful for auditing frontier AI models. However, we do not evaluate LPF against baselines in a realistic auditing setting, so further work is needed to determine its practicality.
title: Uncovering Hidden Behaviours in Language Models via Limited-Parameter Finetuning

abstract: Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support another. We apply the weight-space intervention paradigm of ROME and MEMIT at the granularity of one MLP down-projection column. Our measurement, Empirical Margin Sensitivity (EMS), replaces each coordinate magnitude of a column by its mean while preserving the column's sign pattern and L1 scale, and records the resulting change in the logit margin between the correct option and its hardest-wrong competitor. This isolates the margin's dependence on a column's fine-grained coordinate structure while the column stays in place. We discover high-EMS columns (anchors) on MedQA in ten public checkpoints (four general-purpose bases and six medical post-trained variants) across the Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM families, and measure the same columns on MedMCQA and PubMedQA. Mean-ablating each discovered anchor set lowers MedQA accuracy in all six post-trained models, by 6 to 28 points. In the two pure-SFT checkpoints, crushing anchors raises the PubMedQA margin on correctly answered items (negative EMS), and anchors with this property sit significantly deeper than the same model's other anchors; the four checkpoints trained with RL or mixed recipes show positive PubMedQA EMS and no significant depth shift. The depth association recurs in each of three held-out checkpoints. Because the checkpoints differ in data and pipeline as well as objective, we report these as per-checkpoint observations.
title: Empirical Margin Sensitivity: An Interventional Neuron-Level Probe of Post-Trained Medical LLMs

abstract: Long-term time series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, weather and finance, where forecasts are produced continuously and often on constrained hardware. Recent work has moved in two directions. One scales Transformers and pre-trained foundation models to millions or hundreds of millions of parameters. The other shows that models with only hundreds to tens of thousands of parameters remain competitive on the standard benchmarks. Existing surveys organize forecasting models by backbone and treat efficiency as a side topic, so the reasons these small models work, and the way their sizes are reported, remain unexamined. This survey focuses on lightweight long-term forecasting. It provides a taxonomy of about thirty-five models in six families, with a common notation and an architecture diagram for each core model. It offers a structured-linear view in which the smallest models are linear maps restricted by frequency truncation or period folding, and it tests each restriction in closed form on eight benchmarks. It complements the literature review with an audit of sixteen official code repositories, which reproduces published parameter counts and reveals reporting gaps of up to 289 times. Finally, it gives practical guidance on model selection and reporting, and summarizes open problems.
title: How Many Parameters Does Forecasting Need? A Survey and Code-Level Audit of Lightweight Long-Term Time Series Forecasting

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations, but repeatedly including multiple examples increases context length and inference cost. Many existing implicit ICL methods encode demonstrations as fixed vectors, limiting adaptation of the intervention to individual queries and token positions. We propose Attention-Patching, an implicit ICL method that models contextual changes in self-attention outputs through task-specific updates to attention output projections. Using query-answer pairs processed with and without a fixed demonstration set, Attention-Patching fits layer-wise affine transformations from non-contextual attention representations to the demonstration-induced output changes. Across 12 classification benchmarks and four model families, Attention-Patching achieves higher average accuracy than the evaluated implicit ICL baselines while maintaining performance comparable to explicit ICL at near zero-shot inference cost. Further experiments on diverse generation tasks demonstrate its applicability to autoregressive multi-token generation.
title: Learn the Effects, Not the Examples: Implicit ICL via Attention Patching

abstract: Speech synthesized by text-to-speech engines is a low-cost substitute for recorded test sets in automatic speech recognition, yet an off-the-shelf synthetic test set is worth only a few dozen real recordings for estimating the real error rate of a recognizer. This paper examines which properties of real recordings are missing from synthetic speech and how much of the gap can be closed. For 507 Turkish Common Voice recordings, synthetic twins are built: a ladder of synthetic copies that adds, one factor at a time, the pitch of the speaker, a clone of the same speaker, the real recording channel and the speaking rate. At each step, the agreement between ASR behaviour on the copy and on the real recording is measured. Across three zero-shot cloning engines and panels of six and 19 recognizers, the speaker clone is the step that improves agreement on which sentences are hard, raising the Spearman correlation from .41 to .55 for Chatterbox. Matching the channel or adding generic noise corrects the error level when the synthetic speech is easier than real speech. The twin with the highest worth is equivalent to 70 to 122 real recordings, depending on the recognizer panel, compared with about 9 for a stock voice. The findings replicate on VoxForge, a second corpus in which speaker identity is known rather than inferred: the clone raises sentence agreement from .31 to .50 and the worth from 8 to about 50 recordings. Agreement on which sentences are hard is distinct from agreement on how hard they are. The paper concludes with a practical recipe and a reporting checklist for synthetic ASR test sets.
title: Synthetic Twins: Closing the Gap Between TTS Test Sets and Real Recordings in Turkish ASR Evaluation

abstract: When RL learns from the reactions of many users, the policy usually cannot see what each user wants. We ask what it learns from users who privately want validation: to validate them alone (targeting), or to lower its bar for endorsing everyone (a threshold shift). We answer this in one setting, empathetic RL against LLM-simulated users (RLVER, GRPO, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct): we vary only the share of validation-seeking users (0--50%; RLVER's default: 24.6%) and evaluate on 1,000 Reddit AITA posts with community fault verdicts. The policy shifts its threshold. Endorsement of at-fault posters rises by 3--4 percentage points per 10 points of share; without such users the Qwen model stays at base, and the effect persists at matched KL and under a goal-blind reward. Signal-detection analysis shows that the criterion for endorsing falls while discrimination between at-fault and not-at-fault posters does not decline. An explicit request to be told if one is wrong gives no measurable protection: at-fault posters who make it receive nearly the same rise as those who do not (+0.11 vs. +0.13). When the goal is stated during training, the policy instead largely targets, endorsing seekers regardless of fault. Standard sycophancy and empathy benchmarks miss the shift; five of six usable released empathetic-RL checkpoints also endorse at-fault posters who ask for honesty more than their base models, though a pre-registered prediction for two held for only one. The user mix is a training hyperparameter to audit and report.
title: Lowering the Bar for Everyone: Hidden Validation-Seeking Goals in Empathetic RL

abstract: As a critical functionality of structural health monitoring (SHM) systems, early warning of increased bridge failure risk is essential for structural safety. However, traditional methods treat early warning merely as passive detection against a fixed safety limit and neglect evolving uncertainties and the economic consequences of decisions, leading to delayed alarms that increase the failure risk and hinder reliable and rational decision-making. This study formulates the early warning of increased structural failure risk as a sequential decision-making problem and develops a Bayesian framework for its solution. The presented framework unifies a probabilistic state transition model, an observation prediction model, cost models for early warning decisions, and a threshold-based decision strategy into a closed loop encompassing update, prediction, optimization, and decision execution. The structural state is updated iteratively via Bayes' theorem upon the arrival of new monitoring data, ensuring each decision is conditioned on the latest information. Through pre-posterior analysis over predicted future observations, the warning threshold is optimized by minimizing the expected total cost, which explicitly balances structural failure risks against warning response costs. In this way, the warning paradigm is shifted from passive detection to proactive decision-making, with the warning threshold adaptively updated as uncertainties and costs evolve. The framework was verified via two bridge case studies covering typical scenarios that lead to increased structural failure risk, including steel truss member fracture and stay cable rupture. Results demonstrate that warning decisions can be triggered in a timely and effective manner before severe consequences occur.
title: Bayesian sequential decision-making for adaptive early warning of bridge failure risk

abstract: We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle or implicit discourse. We study Soviet comedy quotations that function as memes in Russian-language communication. Off-the-shelf difficulty estimators do not find these passages; current models searching the web find most but not all of them, but their own analyses of the difficulty do not help translation as well as a human-validated one. Given a brief human-validated analysis of why each passage is difficult, older models improve modestly; the strongest current translators (GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5) improve more, and in human evaluation GPT-6 Sol comes close to the approved references on most films. Newer models have thus become much better at using such an analysis while still not reliably producing it themselves. We release (1) a dataset of five films' Russian subtitles with their audience-selected culturally salient passages, human-validated analyses, and reference translations (into English, Galician, and Spanish), together with every full-film LLM translation and evaluation produced in this study; and (2) an item-level MQM-style evaluation protocol that measures translator and evaluator noise to set the number of runs the evaluation needs, and whose automatic version tracks human judgment of these passages, which reference-free neural metrics do not, whether they score the whole text or the passages alone.
title: Hard to Translate, Harder to Detect: Human Analysis Remains Essential in AI Meme Translation

abstract: Agent skills have become the primary vehicle through which agents reuse specialized capabilities, yet public skill marketplaces provide skills with individual items: a query, whether matched through keyword or embedding similarity, returns a list of single skills ordered by relevance or by popularity. Such an interface cannot answer the question a developer actually faces: which set of skills should be installed to cover a task's complete requirement? The highest-ranked skills are often functionally redundant, while capabilities that are genuinely required remain uncovered. In this paper, we argue that skill acquisition should be reframed from ranking to set selection. We propose Skill-Composer, an agent-native framework that selects a non-redundant skill bundle for the user requirement, which aims to cover all available required capabilities and report any gaps. Specifically, it clarifies user requirements into atomic requirement points, retrieves and merges candidate skills across fragmented marketplaces, decomposes each candidate's capabilities, and progressively discards overlapping ones, so that each retained skill provides different capabilities. This moves the decision of which skills to acquire from the developer to the agent itself. We position this reframing and sketch its workflow.
title: Skill-Composer: Requirement-Driven Skill Selection from Multiple Marketplaces

abstract: Repeating rows then selecting originals retains layout-dependent drift despite equal encoding counts. We measure when existing checks fail to establish preservation contracts in fixed quantized KV-cache implementations. In four-bit HQQ axis zero at sixteen cycles, median paired relative-L2 increases over same-shape re-encoding are 7.22 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B and 11.59 for SmolLM3-3B. Matched encoded states cover sixteen shared questions per model at one and sixteen cycles. Axis one matches the shape-preserving control; lazy reorders preserve the initial state. On one known input, fixed update counts retain the difference; preserving group members removes it. Our prefix-view extension passes current-prefix checks yet changes history and next logits in six model/codec settings at residual capacities four and 128. Public lookup reaches this boundary, including one of four precommitted project-new GPU inputs; fixed query swaps isolate a conditional old-history effect. Checkpoint/dense rollback is exact. An explicit delayed lookup client admits a supported 129-token path excluded by native AR on one known context. Failed task-harm expansion precludes population failure-rate or general answer-degradation claims. Native MLX-LM fixtures expose stale caller caches; synchronization restores the tested in-place contract with native computations preserved. In rejection tests, stale callers change logits but not greedy tokens.
title: Testing Quantized KV-Cache Maintenance: Encoding Layout and Historical Restoration

abstract: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.
title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?

abstract: Descriptions of cities are shaped by human experience and institutional narratives. We introduce the SCD City Personality Assessment (SCD-CPA), a method that instantiates document-grounded ChatGPT city personas and interrogates each with an identical 24-statement instrument inspired by the four-pair structure of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. Rather than asking a general-purpose model to characterize cities freely, we configure a separate document-grounded conversational agent for each city and use alternative evidence portraits to compare documentary inputs. The resulting four bipolar dimensions and four-letter summaries use independently defined urban concepts and scoring rules. Tokyo, New York, and Paris form the methodological evaluation (33 assessments across repeated sessions, three GPT-6 effort settings, and alternative portraits): Tokyo's original portrait yielded 85.4% exact within-setting item agreement, while evidence substitutions shifted some dimension strengths. A five-city application to Shanghai, Dubai, Mumbai, Lagos, and Sao Paulo (15 assessments) yielded 77.8% exact and 99.4% within-one-point cross-setting agreement, indicating consistency under the tested configurations. By treating each city conversational agent as a reproducible, evidence-conditioned experimental configuration, SCD-CPA makes documented city-character perceptions comparable and exposes their sensitivity to source selection. Although the documentary evidence is explicitly controlled, the model's internal interpretation of that evidence cannot be fully observed. We also examine the robustness of SCD-CPA across three AI reasoning-effort settings. The observed consistency suggests that the methodology is relatively insensitive to the tested configuration differences and provides a framework for evaluating its stability as future generations of AI models become available.
title: Can Cities Have Personalities? Introducing the SCD City Personality Assessment

abstract: Human visual intelligence enables efficient reasoning capabilities on abstract visual problems with bounded cognitive resources and minimal experience, and yields remarkable generalization to novel problems with its ability to draw relational analogies and modular abstractions. In contrast, deep learning models require exhaustive task-specific training on large datasets, making them prone to exploiting visual shortcuts and resulting in poor generalization. While neuro-symbolic approaches attempt to bridge this gap by decoupling perception from reasoning with dedicated computation units, existing solutions rely either on explicit rule supervision or parameter-heavy transformer architectures that reintroduce the computational inefficiencies they aim to solve. We introduce Slot-Dwn to address these limitations, a novel neuro-symbolic architecture that unifies unsupervised object-centric perception with logic-based symbolic reasoning. Our model utilizes a Multi-Head Differentiable Weightless Network (MH-DWN) that performs efficient reasoning entirely in Boolean space using look-up tables (LUTs). Our framework reduces visual perception complexity and introduces a LUT-based relational bottleneck with sparse input routing to minimize computational overhead. We evaluate Slot-Dwn across various abstract visual reasoning benchmark tasks targeting systematic rule generalization, sample-efficient anomaly detection, and multi-relational reasoning. We demonstrate that Slot-Dwn yields competitive performance with respect to the state-of-the-art, under extreme out-of-distribution regimes, while requiring up to 52% fewer trainable parameters, with significantly faster convergence.
title: Object-Centric Differentiable Logic Networks for Abstract Visual Reasoning

abstract: In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.
title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. We derive the exact asymptotic bias and give a chain of checks from identification to simultaneous ranks. On a four-agent semi-synthetic benchmark, a scalar correction with oracle calibration has maximum bias 0.245 and mean pointwise coverage 0.016, and never recovers the full ranking (0/250 replications). Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with a uniform or a design-aware random audit keeps the maximum bias below 0.003, with mean pointwise coverage of 0.939 and 0.950. In a 48-cell stress test, effective target support rises only from 0.209 to 0.805 as calibration grows from 600 to 4,800 labels, while audited AIPW keeps a mean absolute error of 0.018-0.020. Without calibration support, or with judge dependence within an externally justified bound, we report valid bounds or sensitivity sets and carry them into rank sets. An e-process confidence sequence stays valid, for a stable target, under predictable adaptive auditing and arbitrary stopping.
title: Transport-Safe Evaluation of LLM Agents: Trajectory-Dependent Judge Error and Anytime-Valid Auditing

abstract: LLM agents turn a user's request and retrieved content into tool calls, and a call can reach the wrong recipient, endpoint, file or participant. Argument-level provenance blocks such values when they come from untrusted content, but accepts a trusted value that the user never requested. IntentFlow, a mediation layer between an unmodified planner and its tools, checks each authority-bearing argument against an intent contract and a provenance policy. On a synthetic benchmark of 200 attacks (oracle intent and injection labels, declared roles), attack success falls from 50.5% with provenance alone to 12.0% [8.2-17.2%]; every remaining success alters a content or payload field. IntentFlow wrongly blocks none of 200 paired benign tasks and 4 of 50 hard ones. On 50 trusted-but-unauthorized attacks, provenance-only mediation executes all 50 and IntentFlow none; a CaMeL-style check also blocks all 50 but rejects 16 of 50 benign tasks. On an offline AgentDojo-derived replay, IntentFlow blocks all 20 attacks at 75% benign success, as does a CaMeL-style check; a Progent-style allowlist blocks 19 and keeps all benign tasks. With one live planner and the same oracles, the mediator blocked all 17 corrupted calls proposed in 110 attacks.
title: Intent-Conditioned Argument Mediation for Tool-Using LLM Agents: Blocking Trusted-but-Unauthorized Arguments

abstract: The tools users approve for their AI agents keep changing their JSON input schemas. Of 8 surveyed MCP clients and scanners, none is observed or documented to re-approve a tool whose input schema widens (two not determinable). We define non-amplification over the coordinates visible in the schema (declared arguments and undeclared fields, on effective values) and a re-binding rule decided by subschema inclusion, trusting no field labels by default and conservative up to its checker and tested case analysis. Evidence: a Coq proof of composition; 48 regression tests; an exact-reference benchmark, where the reviewed version of the rule silently re-bound 27 amplifying changes, now fixed; and a pilot on 604 releases of 39 public MCP servers. There, 412 of 580 compatible schema changes widen some coordinate, yet compatibility re-binds them silently. The authors' adjudicated double annotation finds at least 76 that add or widen an authority-bearing argument (66 of the 84 a name-based labeller flags, plus 10 it misses). On existing tools, the rule asks 645 re-approvals, against 1,197 for pinning the input schema (2,004 with descriptions) and 617 for compatibility. Behaviour change behind an identical schema remains out of reach.
title: SchemaCaps: When a Compatible Tool Update Silently Widens an AI Agent's Authority

abstract: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.
title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.
title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance

abstract: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the environments and write gameplay scripts, producing GameDojo-Data with 600 hours of gameplay trajectories. Experiments reveal substantial challenges for frontier models, especially in real-time interaction. Training on GameDojo-Data brings GameDojo-4B to frontier performance, with the strongest real-time performance. We also find joint training improves individual tasks, and learned policies transfer across bosses. Together, these findings establish GameDojo as a challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community. Our project page is at https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and our code is at https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo .
title: GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games

abstract: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. The framework is designed with three key objectives: (i) reducing manual annotation by harnessing prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, (ii) flexibly parsing diverse document formats (i.e., HTML, PDF, TXT, and JSON), and (iii) improving accessibility for non-expert users by automatically inducing schemas from document collections, which can then be refined for extraction. We evaluate Trallie with open-weight LLMs on FDA 510(k) documents and on movie and university websites from SWDE. It outperforms previously reported systems when the target attributes are provided for text extraction and is competitive when it must discover attributes for the schema automatically. The project is available at https://github.com/PiSchool/trallie
title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs

abstract: Reconstructing time-resolved three-dimensional (3D+t) cardiovascular flow from sparse planar measurements is challenging because each plane observes only the two in-plane velocity components, on a small part of the volume. We propose a plane-aware neural-field framework that learns a continuous 3D velocity field from space and time coordinates through a per-plane projection, and then investigate the potential benefits of physics constraints. We evaluate the framework on computational aortic and aneurysm datasets, and on planes resampled from a real cardiac 4D Flow MRI scan. A plain multi-layer perceptron (MLP) was more accurate than classical radial basis function (RBF) interpolation on both computational datasets. For the aorta, a physics-constrained SIREN (PC-SIREN) reduced the rRMSE further to $0.3756$, compared with $0.4273$ for the plain MLP and $0.7256$ for RBF, and it was the most accurate model in every anatomical segment of the MRI data. For the aneurysms the plain MLP remained the most accurate model, with an rRMSE of $0.07$ to $0.16$ against $0.55$ to $0.71$ for PC-SIREN. Further experiments investigated scanning configuration, number of scans, and spatial resolution. These findings show that continuous neural fields can reconstruct volumetric cardiovascular flow from sparse planar measurements, and that physics constraints have to be matched to the flow.
title: Reconstructing 3D+t Cardiovascular Flow From Sparse Planar Velocity Fields With Neural Fields

abstract: In this expository paper, we explain how quality engineers can use large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for structured data extraction. We introduce the relevant concepts, discuss structured extraction from a measurement-system perspective, and demonstrate its implementation in R and Python. We then present two freely available web-based applications (apps): (a) extracting information from automotive recall notices and (b) monitoring quality engineering research on arXiv. To ensure the accuracy of our AI-driven structured extraction, human evaluators validated the results. In the first app, four reviewers assessed information extracted from 30 recall notices using two models, with 98.6% of the 720 field-level ratings judged fully correct. In the second app, 21 authors evaluated information extracted from 45 of their arXiv papers. All paper summaries were rated mostly correct or correct, although the evaluations identified problems with some classification fields and mathematical expressions. These results demonstrate the practical potential of structured data extraction while emphasizing the need to validate the extracted information. We make both apps and their source code publicly available so that readers can adapt the approach to their own applications.
title: What Quality Engineers Need to Know About Generative AI: Structured Data Extraction

abstract: Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in a filtered set meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as "How many patients with type 2 diabetes, aged 40 to 70, stopped metformin because their blood sugar stayed high?" An interactive application needs this count in seconds, as the user types the criterion, to decide whether the matching set is worth materializing with a batch pipeline in which an LLM judges the records. Prior approximate query processing over such semantic predicates has an expensive model, the oracle, label a sample at query time, so every query waits for the oracle. We present SignalCount, a production system that answers COUNT queries with structured and semantic predicates and calls no oracle at query time, even for ad-hoc criteria. Its oracle is the production LLM judge, and the judge's logged verdicts calibrate, offline, the fast classifier that already runs in front of the judge. At query time, SignalCount counts the filtered set exactly and draws a uniform sample of at most 1,000 records in one columnar scan, scores the sample with the classifier, and multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact count. Its 90% interval combines a sampling term with one-sided, rate-dependent margins for calibration error, fitted by split conformal prediction across tenants. In a multi-tenant production deployment, latency has a p99 of 3.8 s and stays flat as the filtered set grows beyond the sample. On tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the count that the production pipeline returns in 92% of estimates, although estimates run about 15% high in aggregate, because a calibration nearly unbiased per record is still biased per criterion.
title: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds

abstract: Hyperbolic representations have shown remarkable success on hierarchical and tree-like data, and Transformers have become a central architecture for representation learning. However, a principled construction of hyperbolic Transformers remains challenging because the self-attention layer decomposes into three coupled primitives, transformation, similarity, and aggregation, that should all respect the underlying geometry. Existing hyperbolic Transformer designs are typically built in the Poincaré or Lorentz models, where bounded domains, time-like constraints, tangent-space detours, or projection steps make it difficult to keep the full block intrinsic and scalable. To address this gap, we propose PVFormer, to the best of our knowledge, the first Transformer architecture that operates natively in proper velocity (PV) space. The proper velocity model provides an unconstrained representation of hyperbolic geometry, and PVFormer exploits this structure to redesign the Transformer block in PV space. On the transformation side, we use PV homomorphism transformations to update query and value representations. On the similarity side, we generalize Euclidean inner-product attention with a PV Busemann score inspired by Busemann-based hyperbolic learning and a PV point-to-hyperplane key transformation. On the aggregation side, we replace Euclidean averaging with PV midpoint aggregation and further derive a scalable PV linear attention variant for large graphs. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of PVFormer across graph, text, and vision benchmarks.
title: PVFormer: Proper Velocity Transformer for Stable and Scalable Hyperbolic Representation Learning

abstract: Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.
title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation

abstract: Human-AI interaction depends on systems acting on user intent rather than explicit procedures, even when that intent is incomplete, evolving, or partially communicable. Literature organizing systems by interaction technique, workflow stage, or division of labor, offer limited insight into which facet of intent an interaction mechanism addresses. We introduce a six-facet taxonomy of intent, grounded in philosophical accounts of mind, action, and meaning, and apply it to systems presented in 198 papers from eleven SIGCHI venues. Our analysis reveals that different forms of incomplete intent are associated with distinct interaction and authorship strategies, showing that mechanisms that appear similar often address fundamentally different intent-related problems. This exposes blind spots, as intent is rarely represented as an interaction object, authorship provenance is rarely tracked, and tentative preferences are rarely distinguished from firm commitments. The taxonomy offers a lens for analyzing and designing AI systems around the facets of intent they address.
title: How Systems Treat Intent: A Faceted Taxonomy of Intent for Human-AI Co-Creation

abstract: Precise asymptotic theory for M-estimators in high-dimensional settings is largely limited to convex or mildly non-convex formulations, yet non-convex loss functions as well as regularizers are widely used in practice. We study M-estimation in generalized linear models (GLMs) where the loss function or the regularizer can be non-convex. Under rotationally invariant design matrices in the proportional asymptotic regime, we analyze the problem through Vector Approximate Message Passing (VAMP), whose iterates are described by a low-dimensional deterministic recursion called State Evolution (SE). Existing proofs of SE require the proximal operators of the loss function and the regularizer to be Lipschitz, but a non-convex loss or regularizer can have a discontinuous proximal operator, and the usual Onsager terms in VAMP then miss the contribution of the discontinuities. Assuming that the proximal operators are special functions of locally bounded variation, we derive a correction to the Onsager terms using a distributional Stein's lemma. We prove that SE holds for the corrected VAMP. We apply the theory to analyze group sparse regression with an $\ell_0$-type penalty and to robust regression with the Cauchy loss.
title: Precise Asymptotics of Non-Convex M-Estimators
